storySpine.startingBelief: B.Com and BBA are fundamentally different in content.
storySpine.studentSituation: Student reviews programme documents for JOY University.
storySpine.observation: Both programmes list 'Business Organization & Management' in Semester I.
storySpine.focus: Identifying the scope of shared subject titles.
storySpine.whyQuestionFollows: One title does not confirm identical teaching or assessment depth.
storySpine.changedAction: Replaces degree-title guessing with specific course-detail investigation.
storySpine.visibleConsequence: Student notes the shared row and adds a specific inquiry about depth.
storySpine.channelExperience: Audience sees official source citations correcting an assumption.

candidates.title: The Shared Course Reality
candidates.audienceGap: Believing degree labels dictate every subject's content.
candidates.viewerChange: Understands that titles do not confirm identical academic depth.
candidates.concept: Verification of shared subject titles using official PDFs.
candidates.payoff: Student avoids making degree choices based on misleading label assumptions.
candidates.hlni: Business Organization & Management exists in both programs; labels don't guarantee identical depth. Source: JOY University 2025-26 documents.
candidates.support: Official JOY University PDF, B.Com Accounting & Finance p.5 and BBA Entrepreneurship Management p.9; covers identify the 2025–26-onwards cohort.
methodSteps: Use as a starting point for further inquiry.
candidates.interpretationRule: Shared titles do not establish identical content or depth.
candidates.visibleProof: Comparison of row entries from cited PDFs.
candidates.limitations: Does not prove identical teaching, outcomes, or future semester overlap.

demonstration.observation: Row is present in both B.Com and BBA documents.
demonstration.nextQuestion: How does the focus of this course differ in each?

storySpine.startingBelief: Choosing a degree is a single, final decision.
storySpine.studentSituation: Student is stuck between two degree options.
storySpine.observation: The student has no information on assessment types for either.
storySpine.focus: Distinguishing work product from assessment criteria.
storySpine.whyQuestionFollows: Knowing the task isn't enough to know how it is graded.
storySpine.changedAction: Creates a three-column worksheet to map product, criteria, and feedback.
storySpine.visibleConsequence: Student marks unknown cells and identifies specific questions for the admission team.
storySpine.channelExperience: Audience learns a structured method for evaluating course transparency.

candidates.title: The Assessment Audit
candidates.audienceGap: Assuming task labels equate to assessment transparency.
candidates.viewerChange: Learns to separate task expectations from grading criteria.
candidates.concept: Structured audit of course assessment transparency.
candidates.payoff: Student gains a concrete list of questions to ask faculty.
candidates.hlni: A task label doesn't reveal assessment criteria; separating product, criteria, and feedback is essential for informed choice.
candidates.support: Method separates three independent information variables.
candidates.interpretationRule: Use unanswered cells to guide specific inquiries.
candidates.visibleProof: A three-column question sheet showing gaps.
candidates.limitations: Does not predict aptitude or long-term degree performance.

demonstration.nextQuestion: What is the specific criteria used to grade this?

storySpine.startingBelief: I need to know my degree choice today.
storySpine.studentSituation: Student feels overwhelmed by the B.Com vs BBA decision.
storySpine.observation: Student completes a mini-task and records a specific frustration point.
storySpine.focus: Moving from general anxiety to specific investigation.
storySpine.whyQuestionFollows: General feelings don't lead to research actions.
storySpine.changedAction: Uses the frustration to write a specific question for a course brief.
storySpine.visibleConsequence: Student feels calm after noting a concrete next step.
storySpine.channelExperience: Audience relates to the stress of choice and finds a tool for clarity.

candidates.title: The Clarity Journal
candidates.viewerChange: Recognizes that specific questions replace vague worry.
candidates.concept: Using mini-tasks as a tool for personal inquiry.
candidates.payoff: Student leaves with a clear research task instead of anxiety.
candidates.hlni: An illustrative activity reveals where you need help; it does not measure degree fit, but provides a specific research question.
candidates.support: The observation supports a next question rather than a general prediction.
candidates.interpretationRule: Observations identify where to ask for more info.
candidates.visibleProof: A written note turning a frustration into a question.
candidates.limitations: Does not measure aptitude or predict long-term engagement.

demonstration.observation: I don't understand how to classify this expense.
demonstration.nextQuestion: Can I see the definition list used for this task?

storySpine.startingBelief: I must choose the degree that fits my 'personality'.
storySpine.studentSituation: Student is worried about picking the wrong path.
storySpine.observation: Student lists their preferences but finds they have no verification.
storySpine.whyQuestionFollows: Preference is not confirmation of availability.
storySpine.changedAction: Moves preferences to a 'To Check' list and identifies the required evidence.
storySpine.visibleConsequence: Student stops worrying and starts verifying specific constraints.
storySpine.channelExperience: Audience learns to separate personal desire from factual checking.

candidates.title: The Preference Check
candidates.viewerChange: Learns to list unknowns as verification steps.
candidates.concept: Method of separating desire from factual checking.
candidates.payoff: Student stops guessing and starts confirming.
candidates.hlni: An appealing option is not an available one; unknown requirements must be checked rather than assumed.
candidates.support: The method distinguishes desire from confirmation.
candidates.limitations: Does not create eligibility or admission availability.

demonstration.observation: It is currently a preference, not a confirmed feature.
demonstration.nextQuestion: Where is this feature listed in the curriculum?

storySpine.startingBelief: I can guess the degree by looking at one task.
storySpine.studentSituation: Student sees a business task and tries to guess the degree.
storySpine.observation: The task is unlabeled and lacks institutional markers.
storySpine.whyQuestionFollows: Guessing lacks a factual basis without linked evidence.
storySpine.changedAction: Acknowledges 'Insufficient Information' and asks for the source link.
storySpine.visibleConsequence: Student avoids a forced, incorrect classification.
storySpine.channelExperience: Audience discovers how to handle missing evidence in decision making.

candidates.title: The Labeling Challenge
candidates.audienceGap: Assuming one task is sufficient for identification.
candidates.viewerChange: Learns to identify missing information instead of guessing.
candidates.concept: Identifying information gaps in forced-choice scenarios.
candidates.payoff: Student avoids drawing conclusions from partial data.
candidates.hlni: One unlabeled example cannot prove a degree. A valid conclusion requires linking evidence, not guessing.
candidates.support: Reasoning limit: absent information cannot establish exclusive classification.
candidates.visibleProof: Showing the lack of institutional source on the task.
candidates.limitations: Does not prove the task belongs to either programme.

demonstration.visibleInput: Analyze market trends for local bakery.
demonstration.observation: No source or programme label provided.
demonstration.nextQuestion: Is there a source link for this task?

storySpine.startingBelief: Similar totals mean the experiences are identical.
storySpine.studentSituation: Student compares two degree summaries with equal credit totals.
storySpine.observation: The component list for each is completely different.
storySpine.whyQuestionFollows: Aggregates hide the underlying mix of components.
storySpine.changedAction: Requests a detailed component breakdown before comparing.
storySpine.visibleConsequence: Student chooses to review the mix rather than the number.
storySpine.channelExperience: Audience realizes why summaries can be misleading.

candidates.title: The Total Trap
candidates.audienceGap: Using aggregate numbers to judge course content.
candidates.viewerChange: Learns to look for component breakdowns.
candidates.payoff: Student makes more informed, detailed comparisons.
candidates.hlni: The same total can result from different components; an aggregate alone hides the underlying mix.
candidates.support: The claim follows from the displayed arithmetic.
candidates.visibleProof: Displaying two equal totals with different parts.
candidates.limitations: Does not assign figures to actual university credits.

demonstration.input: Two summary tables with identical totals.
demonstration.observation: The components differ despite equal totals.
demonstration.nextQuestion: Can I see the list of components for these credits?

plan.contrast: Trust uses official document verification for objectivity. Connection uses a peer-based inquiry method for psychological relief. Discovery uses logical reasoning to expose gaps in partial data.

issues: production: The constraint explicitly states that 'a smile, a closed notebook, 'choose better' or a restatement of the method is not a consequence.' Feeling calm is an internal emotional state rather than a visible consequence showing how the insight improves the student's next step. Correction: The student produces a list of specific research questions for an academic advisor.

issues: integrity: The Concept Quality Contract explicitly states that 'Categorising an expense does not lead to auditing a budget.' The student's frustration with expense classification is used as a springboard for a next question, violating the instruction to avoid this specific error. Correction: Replace the expense classification task with an academic task relevant to a B.Com or BBA curriculum, such as analyzing a business organizational structure.
